stories.headline: 10-YEAR TREASURY YIELD TOPS 5.30%, A 24-YEAR HIGH, AS TRADERS LOOK PAST SOFTER PCE
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield climbed roughly 4 basis points to 5.29-5.30% Wednesday, its highest level since spring 2002, even after the PCE price index — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — rose a milder-than-expected 0.3% for the month. The S&P 500 slipped 0.25% to 7,652 as the long end of the curve kept grinding higher into Friday's jobs report.
stories.explain: Yields usually fall when inflation data comes in soft, since that lowers the odds of further Fed tightening, but the 10-year rose anyway because term premium — the extra yield investors demand to hold longer-dated debt — is being pushed up by a fresh government shutdown and mounting Treasury issuance to fund the deficit, concerns that sit on top of near-term inflation expectations rather than being solved by one data point. Because the 10-year sets the benchmark rate for mortgages, corporate bonds and equity discount rates, a 24-year high here tightens financial conditions economy-wide even while the Fed hasn't moved its policy rate at all.

stories.headline: GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN BEGINS — THE 22ND SINCE 1976 — AS MARKETS LARGELY SHRUG IT OFF
stories.body: The federal government shut down Wednesday after Congress failed to pass funding legislation, marking the 22nd lapse since 1976. Stocks showed little reaction — history shows equities have posted gains during more than half of the prior 21 shutdowns — but a prolonged lapse risks delaying key data releases, including Friday's jobs report.
stories.explain: Shutdowns furlough federal workers and pause non-essential agency functions, but they don't touch Social Security, Medicare or debt service, which is why equity markets typically treat them as noise rather than a solvency event. The bigger risk to traders right now is informational, not fiscal: if the Bureau of Labor Statistics can't publish Friday's payrolls report on schedule, the Fed and the market lose a data point right as they're trying to judge whether the labor market justifies the 10-year's climb to 5.30%.

stories.headline: DOW POSTS WORST MONTH IN YEARS AS S&P 500 CLOSES A LOSING SEPTEMBER, NASDAQ BUCKS THE TREND
stories.body: The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 443.87 points (-0.86%) to 50,906.05 Wednesday and closed out September down 4.9% for the month, while the S&P 500 finished the month down 0.7%. The Nasdaq 100 was the outlier, rising 0.37% Wednesday to 30,453 and gaining 1.7% for September on renewed AI-trade buying.
stories.explain: The divergence comes down to duration and composition: the Dow's industrial and financial names are more directly exposed to rising borrowing costs and a cooling consumer — University of Michigan sentiment hit a 12-year low this week — while Nasdaq 100 mega-caps have earnings growth strong enough to partially offset a higher discount rate. When short-term inflation data improves but long yields keep rising anyway, it's typically the most rate-sensitive, debt-heavy sectors that lag, which is exactly the pattern separating the Dow from the Nasdaq this month.

stories.headline: BRENT CRUDE SURGES 14% IN SEPTEMBER AS IRAN-HORMUZ STALEMATE DRAGS ON
stories.body: Brent crude rose 0.9% Wednesday to settle at $103.50 a barrel, capping a 14.4% monthly gain, while WTI was roughly flat at $90.31 (-0.1%) but still up 5.3% for the month. Trump said the U.S. now has "almost total control" of the Strait of Hormuz, even as formal U.S.-Iran talks to reopen it remain stalled.
stories.explain: Brent and WTI are diverging because Brent is the global waterborne benchmark most exposed to Middle East supply risk, while WTI is more insulated by landlocked U.S. shale production that doesn't need to transit Hormuz — so a stalemate over the strait shows up disproportionately in the Brent-WTI spread. Roughly a fifth of global oil consumption passes through Hormuz, so futures are pricing the probability-weighted risk of prolonged disruption rather than any actual change in current flows, which is why prices can stay elevated even as Trump claims oil is still moving through the strait.

stories.headline: GOLD REBOUNDS 1.4% TO $4,185 AS WEAK DATA COOLS FED HIKE BETS
stories.body: Spot gold climbed 1.4% to around $4,185 an ounce Wednesday, even as the Dollar Index (DXY) eased 0.11% to 101.26 on signs the softer PCE print reduces the odds of another near-term Fed rate hike.
stories.explain: Gold and the dollar are moving in their usual inverse relationship here: softer inflation data lowers the expected path of real interest rates, which reduces the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset like gold while also taking some pressure off the dollar's rate-advantage bid. The rebound also reflects safe-haven demand tied to the shutdown and the Hormuz standoff — gold tends to catch a bid whenever policy uncertainty rises, even on a day when the stock-bond "risk-off" signal is otherwise mixed.

stories.headline: 101 DAYS TO TIP-OFF: DUKE'S SCHEDULE LOOMS BRUTAL, FLORIDA'S GOLDEN CHASES A REPEAT TITLE
stories.body: With the 2026-27 season about 101 days out, Duke Basketball Report flagged a brutal slate that includes ACC rivals Louisville, Virginia, Miami and UNC plus nearly half of Busting Brackets' 25 Final Four contenders. Florida coach Todd Golden is positioning to chase back-to-back national titles, while Tennessee transfer Jalen Haralson looks to expand beyond the point-guard role he was boxed into at Notre Dame.

stories.headline: CURRY SIGNS BELOW-MAX $112M WARRIORS EXTENSION AS TEAMS OPEN TRAINING CAMP
stories.body: Stephen Curry signed a below-the-max, two-year, $112 million extension to stay in Golden State as all 30 teams opened training camp this week with no games yet on the schedule. Elsewhere, Suns forward Dillon Brooks was charged with DUI stemming from a March arrest, and D'Angelo Russell signed with the Shanghai Sharks after being waived by Memphis.

stories.headline: DOLPHINS' ACHANE OUT FOR SEASON WITH TORN ACL AS FALCONS LOCK UP DEXTER FOR $78M
stories.body: Miami running back De'Von Achane suffered a season-ending torn ACL, a major blow to a Dolphins offense already fighting to stay afloat. Atlanta signed DT Gervon Dexter to a four-year, $78 million extension ($46.5 million guaranteed), while Patriots QB Drake Maye (shoulder) and Vikings WR Justin Jefferson (ankle) both landed on injury reports ahead of the weekend.

stories.headline: TEXAS HOLDS NO. 1 AT 4-0 AS CFP MODEL GIVES SEC A 39% TITLE SHOT OVER BIG TEN'S 38%
stories.body: Texas remains the unanimous No. 1 in both major polls at 4-0 as September wraps up, with ESPN's model giving the SEC a 39% chance at the national title and the Big Ten 38%, Ohio State the single best bet at 17%. Georgia needed back-to-back Austin Romaine pick-sixes to escape with a 41-13 win over Oklahoma, and Iowa preps to host No.-ranked Ohio State Saturday after surviving Michigan.

deepDive.title: Why the 10-Year Treasury Yield Just Hit a 24-Year High
content: Wednesday's 10-year Treasury yield print — above 5.30%, the highest since spring 2002 — landed on the same day the PCE index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, came in softer than expected at 0.3% for the month. That's a strange pairing at first glance: milder inflation data should, all else equal, lower the expected path of Fed policy and pull yields down. Instead, yields rose. Understanding why requires separating what drives short-term rate expectations from what drives the price of a bond that won't mature for a decade.

The mechanism is term premium — the extra compensation investors demand to hold long-dated debt instead of rolling over short-term bills, above and beyond where they expect the Fed funds rate to average over that horizon. Term premium isn't set by this month's CPI or PCE print; it moves with supply and demand for duration itself. Wednesday brought two fresh sources of upward pressure on it: a government shutdown that raises near-term uncertainty about fiscal management, and the market's ongoing digestion of heavy Treasury issuance needed to fund a persistent federal deficit. Both push investors to demand more yield for locking up money long-term, regardless of next month's inflation trajectory.

What's easy to miss is that this is functionally the same dynamic that drove the 30-year to its own multi-decade highs earlier this year during the Iran-driven oil spike — a geopolitical or fiscal shock raises the risk premium on long duration even while short-term inflation expectations stay anchored. The 2003 Treasury market saw a similar disconnect: the 10-year rose sharply even as the Fed held rates near zero, purely on worries about deficit-driven issuance. History's lesson is that term premium spikes are notoriously sticky — they don't reverse just because one data point improves; they need the underlying fiscal or political uncertainty to resolve.

For Chris, the read-through connects directly to today's other headlines: gold's 1.4% rally and the Dow's underperformance versus the Nasdaq both trace back to this same term-premium story. Gold is catching a safe-haven bid because a shutdown-and-issuance-driven yield spike is a different, less Fed-controllable kind of risk than a garden-variety inflation scare, and rate-sensitive Dow components are lagging precisely because their valuations depend more heavily on the level of long-term rates than mega-cap tech's do. Watch whether Friday's jobs report, if it isn't delayed by the shutdown, gives the Fed enough cover to jawbone term premium back down — or whether a prolonged funding lapse keeps pushing it higher into October.
